clinicalPearls: Consider in a premenopausal woman with progressive breathlessness, recurrent pneumothorax, or unexplained diffuse cystic lung disease
High-resolution imaging shows numerous thin-walled, round cysts distributed diffusely throughout otherwise normal lung
LAM occurs sporadically and in association with tuberous sclerosis complex, so examine for skin, renal, and neurological features of that condition
Renal angiomyolipomas and chylous pleural effusions or ascites support the diagnosis
A raised serum VEGF-D level can support the diagnosis non-invasively in the right clinical context
mTOR inhibition is the recognised disease-modifying therapy for progressive disease and for symptomatic angiomyolipomas and chylous complications
Disease may worsen with oestrogen exposure, and pneumothorax can be recurrent and difficult to manage
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis is driven by inactivating mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 tumour suppressor genes, which normally restrain the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. Loss of this control leads to abnormal proliferation of smooth-muscle-like LAM cells that infiltrate the lung, airways, lymphatics, and blood vessels. These cells drive cystic destruction of lung parenchyma and obstruction of lymphatics, producing progressive airflow obstruction, cyst formation prone to rupture, and chylous fluid collections; the same pathway dysregulation underlies associated renal angiomyolipomas.
additionalDifferentials: Emphysema, especially in younger or non-smoking patients
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution chest computed tomography to characterise cysts
Abdominal imaging for renal angiomyolipomas and lymphatic masses
Assessment for tuberous sclerosis complex including skin, brain, and genetic evaluation
Pulmonary function tests, typically showing obstruction with reduced gas transfer
Pleural fluid analysis for chyle where an effusion is present
redFlags: Rapidly declining lung function or worsening hypoxaemia
Large chylous effusion causing respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: The course is variable but generally slowly progressive; mTOR inhibition can stabilise lung function and shrink angiomyolipomas, and with modern management many patients maintain function for years, though some progress to respiratory failure requiring transplantation.
pitfalls: Dismissing diffuse cystic change in a young woman as emphysema
Failing to screen for tuberous sclerosis and renal angiomyolipomas
Overlooking VEGF-D testing that could avoid a lung biopsy
Not counselling about oestrogen exposure and pneumothorax recurrence risk
references: ATS/ERS clinical practice guideline on lymphangioleiomyomatosis
management: mTOR inhibition with sirolimus (or everolimus) as disease-modifying therapy for declining lung function, chylous complications and renal angiomyolipomas
Bronchodilators for airflow obstruction, supplemental oxygen and pulmonary rehabilitation for symptomatic support
Avoid oestrogen-containing therapies and counsel on the risks of pregnancy
Manage recurrent pneumothorax with drainage and early pleurodesis given the high recurrence rate
Treat renal angiomyolipomas with mTOR inhibition or selective arterial embolisation to prevent haemorrhage
Monitor with serial pulmonary function tests and screen for tuberous sclerosis complex, with genetic counselling where it is confirmed
Ensure vaccination and refer for lung transplantation assessment in progressive respiratory failure
